I don't want my children to grow up in a world where we're always on the brink of a massive fallout between superpowers.

judgments.opinion: I think the biggest challenge is just safety and stability.
If you're a woman out there, or if you got kids, you're always looking over your shoulder.
Even if the city 'allows' it, it's still a tent.
You can't lock a tent door.
When you're living that close to everyone else's problems—drugs, mental health issues, or just people being desperate—it's hard to feel like you can actually rest.
Another big thing is cleanliness and health.
In those camps, if there aren't enough bathrooms or places to wash your hands, people get sick fast.
It's hard to get your life together or look presentable for a job interview at Wendy's if you haven't had a real shower in a week.
If the city is gonna 'sanction' a camp, they need to provide the basics—clean water, real toilets, and security.
You can't just tell people 'you can stay here' and then walk away.
Instead of making them go across town to some office to get help, the people who help with housing or jobs need to be *at* the camp.
For moms in those situations, they need a safe place for their kids so they can go work or look for an apartment without worrying about what's happening at the camp.
A camp shouldn't be the end of the road.
It needs to be a bridge.
It shouldn't be that hard just to have a safe place to sleep.

missed_opinions: People in those situations need to feel like they're still human; many people are close to being homeless if one thing goes wrong
